So, $m_n = m_n(\\log T_n)$.\n    28\tWe want to find $\\lim_{n \\rightarrow \\infty} \\frac{m_n(\\log T_n)}{(\\log n)^2}$.\n    29\t\n    30\tA standard property of medians is that if a sequence of random variables $X_n$ converges to a constant $L$ in probability, then the median of $X_n$ also converges to $L$. That is, $m_n(X_n) \\to L$ as $n \\to \\infty$.\n    31\tIn our case, $X_n = \\frac{\\log T_n}{(\\log n)^2}$ and $L = \\frac{1}{\\pi}$.\n    32\tTherefore, the median of $X_n$ converges to $1/\\pi$:\n    33\t$$\n    34\t\\lim_{n \\rightarrow \\infty} m_n\\left(\\frac{\\log T_n}{(\\log n)^2}\\right) = \\frac{1}{\\pi}.\n    35\t$$\n    36\tAnother property of medians is that for any constant $a > 0$, $m_n(aY) = a \\cdot m_n(Y)$.\n    37\tIn our case, $a = \\frac{1}{(\\log n)^2}$ (which is positive for large $n$) and $Y = \\log T_n$.\n    38\tSo, we can write:\n    39\t$$\n    40\tm_n\\left(\\frac{\\log T_n}{(\\log n)^2}\\right) = \\frac{m_n(\\log T_n)}{(\\log n)^2} = \\frac{m_n}{(\\log n)^2}.\n    41\t$$\n    42\tCombining these results, we get:\n    43\t$$\n    44\t\\lim_{n \\rightarrow \\infty} \\frac{m_n}{(\\log n)^2} = \\frac{1}{\\pi}.\n    45\t$$\n    46\tThus, the constant $c$ is $1/\\pi$.\n    47\t\n    48\tThe final answer is $\\boxed{\\frac{1}{\\pi}}$.\"\n    49\t\\end{document}\n","message":"49 lines read from file starting from line 1. It is a random variable that depends on the Markov chain and the choice of the starting state. The cover time of a connected undirected graph is the cover time of the Markov chain that takes a random walk on the graph, at each step moving from one vertex to a uniformly-random neighbor of that vertex.[1]\nApplications\n[edit]Cover times of graphs have been extensively studied in theoretical computer science for applications involving the complexity of st-connectivity, algebraic graph theory and the study of expander graphs, and modeling Token Ring computer networking technology.[1]\nIn different classes of graphs\n[edit]A classical problem in probability theory, the coupon collector's problem, can be interpreted as the result that the expected cover time of a complete graph is . Ou&hellip;\n        We construct the analogue of Gaussian multiplicative chaos measures for the local times of planar <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Brownian</span> motion by exponentiating the square root of the local times of small circles. We also consider a flat measure supported on points whose local time is within a constant of the desired thickness level and show a simple relation between the two objects. Our results extend those of Bass, Burdzy and Khoshnevisan and in particular <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">cover</span> the entire $L^1$-phase or subcritical regime. These results allow us to obtain a nondegenerate limit for the appropriately rescaled size of thick points, thereby considerably refining estimates of <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Dembo</span>, <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Peres</span>, <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Rosen</span> and <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Zeitouni</span>.\n      <p class=\"list-title is-inline-block\"><a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.08151\">arXiv:1709.08151</a>\n    <p class=\"title is-5 mathjax\">\n        Second order term of <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">cover</span> time for planar simple random walk\n        We consider the <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">cover</span> time for a simple random walk on the two-dimensional discrete torus of side length $n$.&hellip;\n        We consider the <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">cover</span> time for a simple random walk on the two-dimensional discrete torus of side length $n$. <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Dembo</span>, <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Peres</span>, <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Rosen</span>, and <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Zeitouni</span> [Ann. In this paper, we study the exact second order term. Its leading order in the small epsilon-regime has been established by <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Dembo</span>, <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Peres</span>, <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Rosen</span> and <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Zeitouni</span> [Ann. of Math., 160 (2004)]. Recently, ideas from probability on trees were an important component of the multifractal analysis of <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Brownian</span> occupation measure, in joint work with A. <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Dembo</span>, J. <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Rosen</span> and O. <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Zeitouni</span>. As a consequence, we proved two conjectures about simple random walk in two dimensions: The first, due to Erdős and Taylor (1960), involves the number of visits to the most visited lattice site in the first $n$ steps of the walk. The second, due to Aldous (1989), concerns the number of steps it takes a simple random walk to <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">cover</span> all points of the $n$ by $n$ lattice torus. The same applies to&hellip;\n        Let T(x,r) denote the first hitting time of the disc of radius r centered at x for <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Brownian</span> motion on the two dimensional torus. We prove that sup_{x} T(x,r)/|log r|^2 --&gt; 2/pi as r --&gt; 0. The same applies to <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">Brownian</span> motion on any smooth, compact connected, two-dimensional, Riemannian manifold with unit area and no boundary. As a consequence, we prove a conjecture, due to Aldous (1989), that the number of steps it takes a simple random walk to <span class=\"search-hit mathjax\">cover</span> all points of the lattice torus Z_n^2 is asymptotic to (2n log n)^2/pi. Determining these asymptotics is an essential step toward analyzing the fractal structure of the set of uncovered sites before coverage is complete; so far, this structure was only studied non-rigorously in the physics literature. We prove that sup_{x} T(x,r)/|log r|^2 --> 2/pi as r --> 0. The same applies to Brownian motion on any smooth, compact connected, two-dimensional, Riemannian manifold with unit area and no boundary. As a consequence, we prove a conjecture, due to Aldous (1989), that the number of steps it takes a simple random walk to cover all points of the lattice torus Z_n^2 is asymptotic to (2n log n)^2/pi. It is a random variable that depends on the Markov chain and the choice of the starting state. A birds-eye view. The basic approach of this paper, as in [13], is\nto control ǫ-hitting times using excursions between concentric circles. The\nnumber of excursions between two fixed concentric circles before ǫ-coverage\nis so large, that the ǫ-hitting times will necessarily be concentrated near\ntheir conditional means given the excursion counts (see Lemma 3.2).\nThekey idea in theproof of the lower boundin Theorem 1.2, is to control\nexcursions on many scales simultaneously, leading to a ‘multi-scale refine-\nment’oftheclassical secondmomentmethod. Thisisinspiredbytechniques\nfrom probability on trees, in particular the analysis of first-passage percola-\ntion by Lyons and Pemantle [22]. The approximate tree structure that we\n(implicitly) use arises by considering circles of varying radii around different\ncenters; for fixed centers x,y, and “most” radii r (on a logarithmic scale)\nthe discs DT2 (x,r) and DT2 (y,r) are either well-separated (if r d(x,y))\n≪\nor almost coincide (if r d(x,y)). This tree structure was also the key to\n≫\nour work in [13], but the dependence problems encountered in the present\nwork are more severe. While in [13] the number of macroscopic excursions\nwas bounded, here it is large; In the language of trees, one can say that\nwhile in [13] we studied the maximal number of visits to a leaf until visiting\nthe root, here we study the number of visits to the root until every leaf has\nbeen visited. For the analogies between trees and Brownian excursions to\nbevalid, the effect of the initial and terminal points of individual excursions\nmust be controlled. To prevent conditioning on the endpoints of the numer-\nous macroscopic excursions to affect the estimates, the ratios between radii\nof even the largest pair of concentric circles where excursions are counted,\nmust grow to infinity as ǫ decreases to zero.\nSection 2 provides simple lemmas which will be useful in exploiting the\nlink between excursions and ǫ-hitting times. These lemmas are then used\nto obtain the upper bound in Theorem 1.2. In Section 3 we explain how to\nobtain the analogous lower bound, leaving some technical details to lemmas\nwhich are proven in Sections 6-7. In Section 4 we prove the lattice torus\ncoveringtimeconjecture,Theorem1.1,andinSection5weprovetheKesten-\nR´ev´esz conjecture, Theorem 1.4. In Section 8 we consider Brownian motion\non manifolds and prove Theorem 1.3. Complements and open problems are\ncollected in the final section.\n2. To prevent conditioning on the endpoints of the numer-\nous macroscopic excursions to affect the estimates, the ratios between radii\nof even the largest pair of concentric circles where excursions are counted,\nmust grow to infinity as ǫ decreases to zero.\nSection 2 provides simple lemmas which will be useful in exploiting the\nlink between excursions and ǫ-hitting times. These lemmas are then used\nto obtain the upper bound in Theorem 1.2. In Section 3 we explain how to\nobtain the analogous lower bound, leaving some technical details to lemmas\nwhich are proven in Sections 6-7. In Section 4 we prove the lattice torus\ncoveringtimeconjecture,Theorem1.1,andinSection5weprovetheKesten-\nR´ev´esz conjecture, Theorem 1.4.
